claim: Shooting stars are meteors: bits of comet or asteroid debris, often a grain of sand to a pea in size, that vaporize in a bright streak as they hit our atmosphere at tens of thousands of miles per hour.

beats.caption: Specks of comet debris
beats.vo: They're meteors: bits of space rock, often just a grain of sand to a pea in size, left behind by comets like Halley.

beats.caption: Tens of thousands of mph
beats.vo: They hit our air at tens of thousands of miles per hour and vaporize in a bright streak. About forty-eight tons of this stuff falls toward Earth every single day.

beats.caption: Maybe Halley's Comet
beats.vo: So that streak could be a piece of Halley's Comet. Its debris is behind the Orionids every October. What's the brightest one you've ever seen?

sources.text: NASA, Meteors and Meteorites Facts (meteoroids range from dust grains to small asteroids; comet debris mostly grain-of-sand to pea size; Orionids linked to comet Halley; tens of thousands of mph): https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/meteors-meteorites/facts/
NASA, Meteors & Meteorites (about 48.5 tons of meteoritic material falls on Earth each day, almost all vaporized): https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/meteors-meteorites/
